questions.question: What is the difference between localStorage, sessionStorage, and cookies?
questions.title: Local Storage Vs Cookies
questions.direct_answer: All three store client-side data but differ in capacity, lifetime, and transmission. localStorage: ~5-10MB, permanent until cleared, never sent to the server automatically. sessionStorage: same API, ~5MB, per-tab and dies with the tab. Cookies: ~4KB, set with expiry, and sent with EVERY matching HTTP request automatically — the only one the server sees without explicit code, and the only one supporting httpOnly (immune to JS reading).

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: All three store client-side data but differ in capacity, lifetime, and transmission. localStorage: ~5-10MB, permanent until cleared, never sent to the server automatically. sessionStorage: same API, ~5MB, per-tab and dies with the tab. Cookies: ~4KB, set with expiry, and sent with EVERY matching HTTP request automatically — the only one the server sees without explicit code, and the only one supporting httpOnly (immune to JS reading).

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The comparison table, verified:

```
             localStorage   sessionStorage   cookies
capacity     5-10MB         ~5MB            ~4KB
lifetime     forever        tab lifetime     per expiry
sent with    NEVER          NEVER           EVERY matching request
requests
accessible   window JS      window JS       JS (unless httpOnly)
API          sync getItem/  sync             document.cookie or
             setItem                        Set-Cookie header
```

The transmission difference (the decision driver):
```js
// localStorage — client-only state; the server NEVER sees it
localStorage.setItem('theme', 'dark');       // next page load reads it
// every fetch you make: no theme in headers. It's YOUR data.

// cookies — server-visible state, automatic
Set-Cookie: session=abc123; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax
// now EVERY request to this site carries: Cookie: session=abc123
// authentication works because cookies auto-attach — no code needed.
```

When to use each (the interview answer):
- localStorage: preferences, cached data for the UI (theme, recent searches, draft content). Not auth tokens — XSS reads them.
- sessionStorage: per-visit state (wizard step, one-time filters) that shouldn't survive a refresh-in-new-tab.
- cookies: server sessions, CSRF tokens, anything the backend must read. httpOnly beats localStorage for tokens because XSS can't read what JS can't see.

The security angles (the depth): cookies without SameSite are the CSRF vector (a cross-site POST rides your auto-attached cookie); localStorage is the XSS vector (a script injection reads everything). The modern auth pattern: httpOnly + Secure + SameSite=Lax cookie for the session; localStorage only for non-sensitive UI state.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph cookie
        C1[server Set-Cookie] --> B[browser stores]
        B -->|attached to EVERY request| C2[server reads Cookie header]
    end
    subgraph web-storage
        L[localStorage / sessionStorage] --> JS[read only by your JS]
        JS -.never auto-sent.-> X[server never sees it]
    end
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why the 4KB cookie limit exists (the mechanism behind the number): cookies are attached to EVERY matching request — headers, requests for images, scripts, everything. A 1MB cookie would multiply bandwidth across every asset request. The limit is the protocol defending itself. localStorage/sessionStorage live in the browser's storage partition per-origin and are read ONLY by your JS on demand — hence the generous quota.

The storage events (the rarely-known feature): setting localStorage in one tab fires a 'storage' event in OTHER tabs of the same origin — the free cross-tab sync channel. sessionStorage is isolated per-tab (two tabs are different sessions) — the browser treats a duplicated tab as a new session in most browsers, which is the actual semantic people mean by 'per-tab'.

The eviction difference: localStorage persists until explicitly cleared (or quota pressure triggers eviction in some embedded browsers). sessionStorage persists only while its tab lives — including through reloads and restores of that tab. Cookies persist per their expiry: session cookies (no expiry) die with the browser, persistent cookies carry a date. The interview-level subtlety: 'remember me' is implemented by switching from a session cookie to a persistent one — same value, different lifetime attribute.
